n: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for one of the Jewish festivals. John doesn’t name which one; suggestions include Passover, Pentecost, or Tabernacles.

f.g: Unnamed; Jewish men were expected to attend three pilgrimage feasts yearly.

n: Near the Sheep Gate in Jerusalem is a pool called Bethesda, surrounded by five covered colonnades. Archaeologists have uncovered a large double pool matching this description.

f.g: Better “Sheep Gate,” near the temple’s north side, through which sacrificial sheep entered.
Possibly “house of mercy” or “house of outpouring.”
Roofed colonnades.

n: Crowds of sick people lie there — blind, lame, and paralyzed — waiting for the water to stir.

f.g: People without strength — invalids.
Lame.
Paralyzed, with shriveled limbs.

n: This verse explains the popular belief that an angel stirred the water and the first one in was healed. It’s missing from the earliest manuscripts and may have been a later explanatory note. Jesus’ healing doesn’t depend on it.

f.g: Stirred it up — possibly from an intermittent spring feeding the pool.

n: One man there has been disabled for thirty-eight years — longer than many people lived then.

f.g: Illness or disability.
The same length as Israel’s wandering after Kadesh.

n: Jesus sees him lying there, knows how long he has suffered, and asks: Do you want to get well? The question invites the man to hope again.

f.g: Do you want to be healed? Jesus engages the man’s will.

n: The man explains he has no one to help him into the water when it stirs; someone always beats him. After decades, he has no helper and little hope.

f.g: A cry of loneliness as much as a complaint.

n: Jesus commands: Get up, pick up your mat, and walk. No pool, no angel — just His word.

f.w: Rise, take up thy bed, and walk

f.g: A sleeping mat or pallet.

n: Instantly the man is healed, picks up his mat, and walks. Then John adds the detail that sets off the conflict: it was the Sabbath.
The religious authorities confront the healed man: it’s the Sabbath; carrying your mat is against the law. They notice the rule, not the miracle.

f.w: not lawful for thee to carry thy bed
f.g: Jewish tradition listed carrying an object from one domain to another among forbidden Sabbath work.

n: He answers: the man who healed me told me to pick up my mat and walk.

f.g: He defers to the authority of his healer.

n: They demand to know who told him to do that — more concerned about the rule-breaking than the healing.

f.g: They ask about the command, not the miracle.

n: The man didn’t know who it was. Jesus had slipped away into the crowd.

f.g: Did not know.
Slipped away quietly.

n: Later Jesus finds him in the temple: you’ve been healed — stop sinning, or something worse may happen. Spiritual healing matters even more than physical.

f.g: Possibly spiritual or eternal consequences.

n: The man goes and tells the authorities that Jesus was the one who healed him.

f.g: Whether naive or disloyal, his report brings Jesus under scrutiny.

n: From then on the leaders begin persecuting Jesus and seeking to kill Him for doing these things on the Sabbath.

f.g: Not in all manuscripts here, but stated plainly in v. 18.

n: Jesus answers: My Father is working until now, and I am working too. God never stops sustaining creation and doing good, even on the Sabbath — and neither does His Son.

f.g: “Hitherto” means up until now, continually.

n: This makes them even more determined to kill Him: besides breaking their Sabbath rules, He calls God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.
Jesus explains His relationship with the Father: the Son does nothing on His own but does what He sees the Father doing. Joseph Smith taught this reflects the Son following the Father’s pattern.

f.w: what he seeth the Father do

n: The Father loves the Son and shows Him everything He does. Even greater works are coming that will amaze them.

f.g: Giving life and judging — the works described next.

n: Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, the Son gives life to whomever He chooses.

f.g: Makes alive.

n: The Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son.

f.w: committed all judgment unto the Son

n: So that all will honor the Son as they honor the Father. Dishonoring the Son is dishonoring the Father who sent Him.

f.w: honour the Son, even as they honour the Father

n: Whoever hears Jesus’ word and believes the Father who sent Him has eternal life now. They will not be condemned; they have already passed from death to life.

f.w: is passed from death unto life

n: The time is coming — and is already here — when the dead will hear the voice of God’s Son and live. This is true of the spiritually dead now, and of the dead in the spirit world, to whom Christ would preach.

f.w: the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God

n: The Father has life in Himself, and He has granted the Son to have life in Himself too. This is why Jesus could lay down His life and take it up again.
The Father has given Him authority to judge because He is the Son of Man — fully sharing our human experience.
Don’t be amazed: the time is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice. Resurrection is universal.

f.w: all that are in the graves

n: They will come out — those who did good to the resurrection of life, those who did evil to the resurrection of judgment. Pondering this verse led Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon to the vision recorded in D&C 76.

f.g: Damnation here means judgment or condemnation. Joseph Smith was directed to render it “resurrection of the unjust.”

n: Jesus says He does nothing on His own. His judgment is just because He seeks not His own will but the Father’s.

f.w: I seek not mine own will

n: If He alone testified about Himself, His testimony wouldn’t be legally valid. The law required more than one witness.

f.g: Not legally valid on its own.

n: But there is another who testifies about Him, and that witness is true — the Father Himself.

f.w: There is another that beareth witness of me

n: They sent messengers to John the Baptist, and John testified to the truth.
Jesus doesn’t depend on human testimony, but He mentions John’s for their sake, so they might be saved.

f.g: His purpose even in debate is their salvation.

n: John was like a burning, shining lamp, and for a while they were happy to enjoy his light. But their enthusiasm faded.

f.w: a burning and a shining light
f.g: A lamp — lit by another source, unlike Jesus who is the Light itself.
For a while.

n: Jesus has a greater witness than John: the works the Father gave Him to accomplish prove the Father sent Him.
The Father Himself has testified of Him. Yet they have never heard His voice or seen His form — because they did not truly know Him.

f.g: His form or appearance.

n: His word doesn’t live in them, as shown by their refusal to believe the one He sent.

f.g: Remaining, living.

n: They diligently study the scriptures, thinking that study itself gives eternal life — yet the scriptures point to Jesus.

f.g: In Greek this can be a statement (“You search”) or a command.

f.w: they are they which testify of me

n: Yet they refuse to come to Him to receive the life the scriptures promise.

f.w: ye will not come to me

n: Jesus isn’t seeking human praise.

f.g: Glory, approval.

n: He knows them: they don’t have God’s love in their hearts.

f.g: Either love for God or God’s love — probably both.

n: He comes in His Father’s name, and they reject Him; yet if someone comes in his own name, they’ll accept him. History saw many false messiahs welcomed.

f.g: With the Father’s authority, as His representative.

n: How can they believe when they care about each other’s approval but not about the approval that comes from God alone? Seeking praise blocks faith.

f.w: the honour that cometh from God only

n: Jesus won’t need to accuse them before the Father. Moses, in whom they put their hope, will accuse them.

f.g: They prided themselves on following Moses’ law.

n: If they truly believed Moses, they would believe Jesus, because Moses wrote about Him.
But if they don’t believe what Moses wrote, how will they believe what Jesus says? Rejecting the earlier witness leads to rejecting the greater one.

f.w: how shall ye believe my words?
